archetype.name: Playoff Team (possession-first)
archetype.definition: A veteran core that has made a habit of good regular seasons and again controls play at 5-on-5, while the power play and goaltending have not yet caught up to the process.

report.headline: Tampa owns the puck; the power play and Vasilevskiy owe it goals
report.take:
Six games in, Tampa Bay looks like the team it has been for years: one that drives play. The Lightning hold a 57.6 xGF % and a 56 CF % at 5-on-5, both fourth in the league, so this is not a record propped up by bounces. If anything it is the reverse. A 98.7 PDO says pucks are not going in at the rate the chances suggest, and a goal differential of 1 over six games undersells how much of the ice they have tilted.

The record splits neatly. Both losses came at Madison Square Garden, 1-5 and 1-4, and the four games in between were a clean winning streak with Tampa allowing three or fewer every night. The offense sits 20th in goals per game despite the territorial edge. The biggest reason is a power play converting 8.3 percent, 31st in the league. Brandon Hagel has carried the scoring with 27 shots and the No. 4 spot on the winger tab. Kucherov is setting the table with 7 assists, and Guentzel is producing at center. Below that, Point, Cirelli and the bottom six have little to show for good possession numbers.

The goaltending grade is a C. Andrei Vasilevskiy has a .886 save percentage and a slightly negative GSAx through five starts, while Dennis Hildeby was positive in his one. Neither is alarming over this sample. The team GSAx of 0.7 is mid-pack, and Tampa's goalies posted strongly positive GSAx in most recent seasons. The defense around them is good at containing forwards but has let opposing defensemen pile up points, which is worth watching.

The history says this core regresses toward its mean, and here the mean is upward. The power play ran 20.7 percent or better in each of the last five seasons, and last year's team finished fourth on the site. A club sitting 12th while out-chancing nearly everyone is likely to climb once the finishing and special teams normalize.

strengths.title: Controlling play at 5-on-5
strengths.body: Tampa ranks fourth in both expected-goal share and shot-attempt share. Almost every regular forward is above 50 percent on xGF %, so the edge is spread through the lineup rather than leaning on one line. Possession is the stickiest team trait in hockey, and last season's 54 percent xGF share suggests this one is real.

strengths.title: Hagel and Kucherov driving the top
strengths.body: Hagel is shooting at volume and ranks fourth among wingers on the site. Kucherov is the playmaker, with 7 assists and a 65.4 xGF % on his ice time. Hagel's goal pace will cool, but the shot rate that produces it is sustainable.

strengths.title: Smothering opposing forwards
strengths.body: Opposing forwards are scoring well below their own averages against Tampa, with wingers held furthest under. That fits the possession numbers: teams without the puck do not generate much off the rush. It is the base for a defense ranked eighth in goals against per game.

concerns.title: A power play near the bottom
concerns.body: At 8.3 percent, Tampa's power play ranks 31st, and the forward group has only 5 power-play points combined. With Kucherov, Guentzel, Hagel and Point, this is far more likely a slump than an identity. The unit has not finished below 20.7 percent in the five seasons on the sheet, but until it turns, the offense will lag the chances.

concerns.title: Vasilevskiy's slow start
concerns.body: A .886 save percentage and slightly negative GSAx earn the starter a middling tab rank, and the group grade is a C. Five starts are far too few to judge a goalie. Still, the two blowout losses in New York show what happens when the saves do not come behind a team that is otherwise winning its games.

concerns.title: Points leaking to opposing defensemen
concerns.body: Tampa ranks 25th at holding defensemen under their expected output. Blueliners account for a far bigger share of the points against than the league norm. That points to point shots and pinches getting through rather than forwards beating the coverage, and it is fixable but worth tracking.

trend.note: An opening loss in New York, four straight wins, then another loss at the Rangers. The possession numbers have held up throughout, even when the results did not.

weekAhead.headline: Two home games against soft spots, then a real test in Vegas
weekAhead.body:
The week opens with two games in Tampa. Seattle arrives 5-2-0 and eighth on the site, but its 108.3 PDO is running hot on shooting and goaltending, and it sits near the bottom in both xGF % and CF %. That is exactly the kind of team Tampa's possession game should wear down. Vancouver is 2-6-0 with the league's worst penalty kill and goaltending that has cost it goals, a near-ideal opponent for a stalled power play to get going.

The trip to Vegas is the measuring stick. The Golden Knights are fourth on the site, with an A+ forward group and possession shares nearly identical to Tampa's, and they have held opposing centers well under their averages. Taking care of business at home matters, because that last game is close to a coin flip.

keyMatchups.title: Possession against Seattle's hot finish
keyMatchups.body: Seattle has been out-chanced badly at 5-on-5 but is winning on a PDO well above 100. Tampa's shot volume should test whether the Kraken's finishing and A- goaltending can keep it up. This is the clearest regression spot on the schedule.

keyMatchups.title: Tampa's power play against Vancouver's kill
keyMatchups.body: The Canucks kill 57.1 percent of penalties, last in the league, and their goalies are 31st in GSAx. Opposing forwards are piling up points well above their averages against them. If Tampa's power play is going to break out, this is the night.

keyMatchups.title: Centers against Vegas's middle
keyMatchups.body: Vegas has held centers well under their averages, which puts pressure on Guentzel, Point and Cirelli. Combined with an A+ forward group and a 57.3 xGF %, this is the one game where Tampa will not own the puck by default.

weekAhead.watch: Whether the power play scores against Vancouver's league-worst penalty kill: the clearest sign of whether Tampa's goals are about to catch up with its chances.

restOfSeason.body:
The underlying profile is a top-five team at 5-on-5 with a deep, experienced lineup, and that tends to hold. What should change is the finishing. A sub-100 PDO and a power play near the bottom of the league are both far below this core's track record, and both should drift up. That would turn a modest goal differential into a comfortable one. Hagel's goal pace will cool and the depth centers need to start contributing, but the net movement is upward.

The main risk is in net. If Vasilevskiy's early numbers are more than noise, a team that does everything else well becomes merely a playoff team rather than a top-tier one. Six games is a very small sample, so these ranges are wide.
swingFactors: Scoring from Point and the depth centers

confidence.note: Only six games, but possession data and a long, consistent history point the same way.
